subject: religious-studies
title: Applied Ethics: Life and Death
welcome_lead: Take the major normative theories into the clinic and the courtroom to weigh how they handle abortion, euthanasia, and warfare.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on applied ethics in life and death: abortion, euthanasia, and just war theory.
final_note: You have applied Natural Law, Utilitarianism, Kantianism, and Situation Ethics to the hardest cases of life and death.

concepts.def: The principle, rooted in imago Dei doctrine, that human life is intrinsically and inviolably valuable.
The view that some lives are not worth living and may justifiably be ended.
The contested philosophical concept used to identify which beings have moral status.
Bringing about death by direct action.
Allowing death by withdrawing or withholding treatment.
The Christian and Aristotelian framework, articulated by Augustine and Aquinas, specifying jus ad bellum and jus in bello criteria.

walkthroughs.body_html: Natural Law condemns abortion as against the primary precept of preservation. Kantians may invoke the Humanity Formula if the foetus is a person. Utilitarians weigh consequences case by case. Judith Jarvis Thomson's A Defense of Abortion (1971) argues, via her violinist analogy, that even granting personhood, the right to life does not entail the right to use another's body.

James Rachels's Active and Passive Euthanasia (1975) argues there is no moral distinction between killing and letting die. Catholic teaching distinguishes ordinary from extraordinary means: withdrawing burdensome treatment is permissible. Peter Singer, on preference utilitarian grounds, defends voluntary active euthanasia. Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics asks which act is most loving.

The just war tradition, developed by Augustine (City of God) and Aquinas, requires for jus ad bellum: just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, proportionality, reasonable chance of success. For jus in bello: discrimination (between combatants and non-combatants) and proportionality. Pacifists like the Quakers reject war altogether; realists question whether moral criteria apply.
